lessons.title: Tensors
key_points: A tensor is PyTorch's array: numbers arranged in one or more dimensions, like a NumPy array that can also run on a GPU and track gradients.
Every tensor has a shape (for example [32, 4] for 32 rows of 4 features), a dtype (float32 for most model inputs) and a device (cpu or cuda).
Create tensors with torch.tensor(data), torch.zeros(shape) or torch.from_numpy(array). Labels for classification are usually int64 (torch.long).
Operations work element by element (a + b) or as matrix maths (a @ b). Shapes must fit: [32, 4] @ [4, 3] gives [32, 3].
Most bugs in early PyTorch code are shape or dtype mismatches. Print x.shape and x.dtype whenever something fails.

worked_example.title: Turn a small table into tensors
steps: Start with 3 students and 2 features each (hours studied, quizzes done).
x = torch.tensor([[5., 3.], [1., 0.], [8., 4.]]) has shape [3, 2] and dtype float32.
Labels y = torch.tensor([1, 0, 1]) have shape [3] and dtype int64.
A weight matrix w = torch.randn(2, 1) has shape [2, 1], so x @ w has shape [3, 1]: one score per student.
worked_example.code:
import torch

x = torch.tensor([[5., 3.], [1., 0.], [8., 4.]])
y = torch.tensor([1, 0, 1])
w = torch.randn(2, 1)
print(x.shape, x.dtype, y.dtype)   # torch.Size([3, 2]) torch.float32 torch.int64
print((x @ w).shape)               # torch.Size([3, 1])

mini_project.title: Tensor warm-up
mini_project.brief: Get comfortable with shapes before building a network.
steps: Load a small CSV with pandas and convert the feature columns to a float32 tensor.
Convert the label column to an int64 tensor.
Compute the mean of each feature column with x.mean(dim=0) and print its shape.
Make one deliberate shape error with @, read the error message, then fix it.
mini_project.done_when: You can explain the shape of every tensor in your script.

lessons.title: A small neural network
key_points: A neural network is layers of simple functions. nn.Linear(in, out) computes x @ W + b; an activation such as ReLU (max(0, x)) adds the non-linearity that lets the network learn curved boundaries.
In PyTorch you define a network as a class that inherits nn.Module: create layers in __init__ and say how data flows in forward.
The output layer matches the task: one number per class for classification (raw scores called logits), one number for regression.
Calling model(x) runs forward. You never call forward directly.
model.parameters() lists every weight the optimiser will update. Count them to understand the model's size.

worked_example.title: A two-layer classifier for 4 features and 3 classes
steps: First layer: nn.Linear(4, 16) turns 4 features into 16 hidden values.
ReLU sets negative hidden values to 0.
Second layer: nn.Linear(16, 3) gives 3 logits, one per class.
Run a batch of 8 rows through it: the output shape is [8, 3]. The predicted class is the index of the largest logit, logits.argmax(dim=1).

mini_project.title: Design your own network
mini_project.brief: Build the network you will train in the next lesson.
steps: Pick a dataset with numeric features and a class label (iris works).
Write an nn.Module with one hidden layer sized for your features and classes.
Pass one batch through it and check the output shape.
Count the parameters with sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()) and check the number by hand for the first layer.
mini_project.done_when: Your network runs on a batch and you can explain its parameter count.

lessons.title: Training loops
key_points: Training repeats five steps for each batch: predict, compute the loss, clear old gradients, backpropagate, update the weights.
For classification use nn.CrossEntropyLoss, which takes raw logits and int64 class labels. Do not apply softmax first.
The optimiser changes weights to reduce the loss. torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3) is a common starting point.
optimizer.zero_grad() must run before loss.backward(), because PyTorch adds new gradients to old ones.
A DataLoader serves shuffled mini-batches. One pass over all the training data is one epoch; the loss should fall over epochs.

worked_example.title: Train the iris network
steps: Wrap the training tensors in a TensorDataset and a DataLoader with batch_size=16 and shuffle=True.
Create the loss function and the Adam optimiser.
For 50 epochs, loop over the batches: logits = model(xb); loss = loss_fn(logits, yb); optimizer.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); optimizer.step().
Print the average loss every 10 epochs. It should go down; if it does not, check the learning rate and the label dtype.
worked_example.code:
from torch.utils.data import TensorDataset, DataLoader

loader = DataLoader(TensorDataset(X_train_t, y_train_t), batch_size=16, shuffle=True)
loss_fn = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)

for epoch in range(50):
    model.train()
    total = 0.0
    for xb, yb in loader:
        loss = loss_fn(model(xb), yb)
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()
        total += loss.item()
    if epoch % 10 == 0:
        print(epoch, total / len(loader))

mini_project.title: Make the loss go down
steps: Write the training loop with a DataLoader.
Record the average loss per epoch in a list and plot it.
Train again with a learning rate 10 times larger and 10 times smaller, and plot all three curves.
Write one sentence on what the learning rate changed.
mini_project.done_when: You have a plot with three loss curves and a sentence explaining them.

lessons.title: Saving a model
key_points: Before measuring, call model.eval() and wrap prediction in with torch.no_grad(): layers like dropout switch to test behaviour and no gradients are tracked.
Measure on a validation set during training to spot overfitting, and keep the test set for the final score.
Save the learned weights, not the whole object: torch.save(model.state_dict(), "model.pt").
To load, create the same class again, then model.load_state_dict(torch.load("model.pt")) and model.eval().
Save what the model needs to be used later as well: the class names in order and any scaling values used on the inputs.

worked_example.title: Evaluate, save and reload
steps: Switch to evaluation mode and predict the test set without gradients.
Compute accuracy by comparing argmax predictions with the labels.
Save state_dict to model.pt, and the class names to a small JSON file.
In a fresh script, rebuild Net(), load the weights, call eval() and check you get the same accuracy.
worked_example.code:
model.eval()
with torch.no_grad():
    preds = model(X_test_t).argmax(dim=1)
print((preds == y_test_t).float().mean().item())

torch.save(model.state_dict(), "model.pt")

reloaded = Net()
reloaded.load_state_dict(torch.load("model.pt"))
reloaded.eval()

mini_project.title: A model you can hand over
mini_project.brief: Make your trained network reusable by someone else.
steps: Add a validation split and print validation accuracy every 10 epochs.
Save the weights from the epoch with the best validation accuracy.
Save the class names and any input scaling values next to the weights.
Write predict.py that loads everything and predicts one new row given on the command line.
mini_project.done_when: A classmate can run predict.py on your saved files and get a prediction.

check.prompt: x has shape [32, 10] and w has shape [10, 4]. What is the shape of x @ w?
check.explanation: In matrix multiplication the inner sizes (10 and 10) must match and disappear, leaving the outer sizes: [32, 4].

check.prompt: Why does a network need an activation such as ReLU between linear layers?

options.text: To make training faster on a GPU
Without it, stacked linear layers act like one linear layer
To turn the outputs into probabilities

check.explanation: Two linear layers in a row are still a linear function. A non-linear activation lets the network learn curved patterns.

check.prompt: In a training step, what must happen right before loss.backward()?
check.explanation: PyTorch adds new gradients to existing ones, so you clear them with zero_grad before backward. step comes after backward.

check.prompt: What should you pass to nn.CrossEntropyLoss?

options.text: Raw logits and int64 class indices
Predicted class indices and true class indices
Raw logits and float labels between 0 and 1

check.explanation: CrossEntropyLoss applies log-softmax itself, so it takes raw logits, with the true classes as int64 indices.

check.prompt: What is the usual way to save a trained PyTorch model?
check.explanation: The state_dict holds the learned weights. To use them, rebuild the same class and load the state_dict into it.

review_cards.back: A shape, a dtype and a device.

review_cards.back: Predict, compute loss, optimizer.zero_grad(), loss.backward(), optimizer.step().

review_cards.front: What do model.eval() and torch.no_grad() do?
review_cards.back: eval() switches layers like dropout to test behaviour; no_grad() stops gradient tracking during prediction.

review_cards.front: How do you reload saved weights?
review_cards.back: Create the same model class, call load_state_dict(torch.load(path)), then eval().
